title: Global Food Insecurity: Surplus, Deficit & Impacts
description: Why food demand is rising, what restricts supply, and the consequences of global food insecurity.
content_html:
A World Divided by Food

At any given moment, roughly 733 million people do not have enough to eat, yet in wealthy countries a third of all food produced is wasted. This contrast — plenty in some places, food insecurity in others — is one of geography's sharpest inequalities. Geographers map it in terms of surplus and deficit: regions where calorie supply exceeds what people need, and regions where it falls short. Understanding why the gap exists, and what it does to people and landscapes, is the first step toward fixing it.

Key Fact

Around 733 million people worldwide are chronically undernourished (FAO 2024, 2023 data). Sub-Saharan Africa has the highest regional rates of undernourishment — over 20% of the population in many countries. In contrast, North America, Europe and Australasia have dietary energy surpluses, averaging well above the recommended 2,100 kilocalories per person per day.

Global Patterns of Surplus and Deficit

The global pattern of food surplus broadly follows wealth. North America, Europe, Argentina, Brazil and Australasia all have average calorie supplies above 3,000 kcal per person per day — well above the recommended 2,100 kcal. Meanwhile, large parts of sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia and Central America experience food deficit, with averages below 2,000 kcal. The picture is not simply a rich-world versus poor-world divide: parts of South and South-East Asia have grown food-secure as economies developed, while pockets of food poverty remain in parts of southern Europe and the southern United States.

Two main drivers push global food consumption upward:

  • Rising population: the world passed 8 billion people in 2022 and is projected to exceed 9.5 billion by 2050. More people simply means more mouths, and most population growth is concentrated in already-deficit regions of Africa and South Asia.
  • Economic development: as countries grow wealthier, diets shift — people move from staple grains to meat, dairy and processed foods. Producing 1 kg of beef requires roughly 7 kg of grain and large volumes of water, so richer diets place far heavier demands on agricultural systems than subsistence diets do.

In China, meat consumption per person roughly doubled between 1990 and 2015 as hundreds of millions joined the middle class. This single dietary shift required a vast expansion of grain imports (for animal feed) and placed new pressure on global commodity markets. When China buys more soya, prices rise in Brazil's Cerrado, where forests are cleared to grow it. Diet change in one country can drive land-use change thousands of kilometres away — a vivid example of how the global food system is interconnected.

Factors Affecting Food Supply

Even where demand is growing, supply does not always keep pace. Six factors commonly limit food production:

  • Climate: temperature, rainfall and growing season length set the agricultural potential of any region. Drought in East Africa, flooding in Bangladesh or late frosts in the US Midwest can devastate harvests. Climate change is making extreme weather events more frequent, threatening production in the regions least able to cope.
  • Technology: high-income countries use GPS-guided tractors, precision irrigation, disease-resistant crop varieties and cold chains to maximise yields and cut losses. Many LICs lack access to these tools, so yields of staple crops like maize or sorghum can be five to ten times lower per hectare than in HICs growing the same crop.
  • Pests and disease: locusts stripped crops across East Africa in 2020–21, affecting over 23 million people. Plant diseases such as wheat rust and banana wilt, and livestock diseases such as foot-and-mouth, can destroy entire seasons of food production.
  • Water stress: agriculture uses around 70% of all freshwater withdrawn globally. In areas of water scarcity — the Middle East, northern India, the Sahel — farmers cannot irrigate crops, limiting what and how much they grow.
  • Conflict: wars disrupt farming, destroy infrastructure and displace people from their land. In Yemen, South Sudan and Syria, ongoing conflict has contributed directly to widespread famine. Farmers cannot plant or harvest when fighting is happening around them.
  • Poverty: even when food is physically available in a country, poor people may not be able to afford it. Poverty traps — inadequate land, no credit, inability to invest in seeds or tools — mean subsistence farmers stay on the edge of hunger even in relatively fertile areas.

Impacts of Food Insecurity

Food insecurity does not just mean hunger. Its consequences ripple across environments, economies and societies:

  • Famine: the most extreme outcome. Famine occurs when food insecurity becomes so severe that death rates rise significantly. The UN declared a famine in parts of South Sudan in 2017. Famines today are rarely caused by absolute food shortage — they are usually the result of conflict preventing access to food.
  • Undernutrition: chronic food deficits cause stunting in children, weakened immune systems and reduced cognitive development. Globally, around 149 million children under five are stunted. The economic cost is enormous — undernourished workers are less productive, perpetuating poverty cycles.
  • Soil erosion: when food is scarce, people over-farm land — removing trees for fuel, grazing livestock on fragile soils, tilling steep slopes. This degrades the land's future productivity, creating a downward spiral. The UN estimates that around 25 billion tonnes of fertile soil are lost each year to erosion, much of it in food-deficit regions.
  • Rising prices: global food prices spiked sharply in 2007–08 and again in 2010–11, driven by poor harvests, rising fuel costs and speculation. These price shocks hit the poorest populations hardest because they spend a higher share of income on food — in many African countries, over 50% of household income goes on food.
  • Social unrest: high food prices and shortage trigger protests and political instability. The 2010–11 Arab Spring was partly fuelled by rising bread prices. In 2022, food price shocks linked to the Ukraine conflict contributed to political crises in Sri Lanka and Pakistan.
Key Fact

Food insecurity causes famine, stunts the development of 149 million children under five, drives soil erosion that strips 25 billion tonnes of topsoil a year, triggers price spikes that hurt the poorest most, and contributes to political instability and social unrest.

Conflict causes food insecurity by disrupting farming and supply chains, but food insecurity also causes conflict by inflaming grievances over land, water and resources. This feedback loop is clearest in the Sahel region of Africa, where climate-driven drought has reduced pasture, pushing nomadic herders onto cropland and sparking violent clashes with farming communities. Breaking the cycle requires both peacebuilding and agricultural investment — neither alone is sufficient.

Why This Matters

Food insecurity is not an inevitable fact of geography — it is the outcome of decisions about investment, trade, conflict and climate policy. The next lesson explores the strategies being used to close the gap: from large-scale irrigation schemes to urban rooftop farms, and from biotechnology to the simple wisdom of eating seasonally and wasting less.
exam_tip_html: For 4-mark 'Explain' questions on factors affecting food supply, pick two factors and give a clear cause-and-effect chain for each: 'Conflict in Yemen destroyed irrigation infrastructure, preventing farmers from growing crops and leaving millions dependent on food aid.' For 9-mark 'Assess' questions on food insecurity impacts, rank the impacts — famine is the most severe but affects fewer people than chronic undernutrition; soil erosion creates a long-term threat. Examiners reward specific facts (149 million stunted children, 25 billion tonnes of topsoil lost a year) over vague generalisations.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Global food surplus is concentrated in wealthy regions (North America, Europe, Australasia) while deficit is worst in sub-Saharan Africa and parts of South Asia, driven by rising population and shifting diets from grains to meat.
  • Food supply is limited by climate, technology gaps, pests and disease, water stress, conflict and poverty — often acting together in the most food-insecure countries.
  • Food insecurity causes famine, undernutrition in 149 million children, soil erosion, food price spikes and social unrest — making it both a humanitarian and a political crisis.

glossary_terms.definition: A state in which people do not have reliable access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food to maintain a healthy and active life.
A situation in which a country or region produces more food than its population needs, with calories available per person comfortably exceeding the daily requirement.
A situation in which a country or region cannot produce or access enough food to meet the daily calorie needs of its population.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a cause of food insecurity?
A) High crop yields
B) Falling global population
C) Water stress reducing irrigation
D) Declining meat consumption
practice_questions.marks: C) Water stress reducing irrigation [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline two reasons why global food consumption is rising.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per reason with brief development. Examples: rising global population (world passed 8 billion in 2022, most growth in deficit regions); economic development shifting diets from staple grains to meat and dairy (1 kg of beef requires roughly 7 kg of grain); urbanisation increasing demand for processed food; rising incomes in countries like China increasing per-person calorie consumption.

practice_questions.text: Describe the global pattern of food surplus and deficit.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: identifies surplus regions (North America, Europe, Australasia, parts of South America) with average calorie supply above 3,000 kcal, and deficit regions (sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, parts of Central America) below 2,000 kcal, noting the pattern broadly follows wealth. Secure: identifies the surplus and deficit regions with one named example each. Developing: vague claim about 'rich countries having more food'. Emerging: states there is an unequal distribution without describing the pattern.

practice_questions.text: Explain how conflict can lead to food insecurity.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: full causal chain — conflict prevents farmers planting and harvesting, destroys irrigation and storage infrastructure, displaces people from agricultural land, cuts transport routes so food cannot reach markets, and diverts government spending from agriculture to military. Named example: Yemen, South Sudan or Syria. Secure: one clear mechanism with example. Developing: states conflict 'makes farming harder' without mechanism. Emerging: vague link between conflict and food.

practice_questions.text: Suggest how food insecurity can cause social and environmental problems.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three developed points covering both social and environmental — social: price spikes hit poorest households (over 50% of income on food in many African countries); food riots and political instability (Arab Spring 2010–11); chronic undernutrition stunts children's development (149 million children under five). Environmental: over-farming depletes soil (24 billion tonnes of topsoil lost per year); deforestation to open new farmland; over-grazing degrading pasture. Secure: two clear points with evidence, covering at least one social and one environmental. Developing: lists problems without development. Emerging: one vague point.

practice_questions.text: Assess the extent to which climate is the most important factor affecting food supply.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument acknowledging the power of climate (drought, flooding, extreme heat reducing yields, climate change increasing frequency of extreme events) but weighing it against other factors — conflict (famine in Yemen and South Sudan caused by war, not climate), poverty (farmers lack seeds, tools and credit even in fertile areas), technology (HIC yields 5–10 times higher per hectare than LIC), water stress (70% of global freshwater used in farming), pests and disease (East Africa locust crisis 2020–21 affected 23 million). Reaches a justified judgement (e.g. 'climate sets broad boundaries but poverty and conflict turn a poor harvest into a famine'). Secure: two-sided argument with two factors compared. Developing: lists factors with limited evaluation. Emerging: agrees or disagrees without comparison.

knowledge_checks.q: Roughly how many people are chronically undernourished worldwide?
Which region has the highest rates of food insecurity and undernourishment?
Producing 1 kg of beef requires roughly _____ kg of grain, meaning richer diets place far heavier demands on agricultural systems.
The UN estimates around _____ billion tonnes of fertile topsoil are lost to erosion globally each year, much of it in food-deficit regions.
Match each impact of food insecurity to its description.
right: Extreme shortage causing significantly higher death rates, often linked to conflict
Stunted growth and weakened immune systems in around 149 million children under five
Food price spikes triggering protests and political instability, as in the 2010–11 Arab Spring

hero_image_caption: Cracked, parched farmland in a drought-affected region illustrates the environmental conditions that drive food insecurity across sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a food deficit region?
flashcard_questions.a: A region where calorie supply per person falls below what the population needs.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two global regions that experience food surplus.
flashcard_questions.a: North America and Europe (also accept Australasia or Argentina/Brazil).

flashcard_questions.a: Rising population and economic development shifting diets toward meat and dairy.

flashcard_questions.q: How much grain is needed to produce 1 kg of beef?
Name three factors that limit food supply.
flashcard_questions.a: Climate, conflict and poverty (also accept technology gaps, pests and disease, water stress).
